name: Hair styling clay & pomade

lead: Hair clay and pomade shape and hold hair so a cut looks neat and styled all day. Pomade is traditionally greasy, waxy or water-based and gives a shiny, slick finish; clay is a related styling paste with a more matte, textured look. Both appear in grooming discussions as tools for the pompadour, quiff and textured crop.

Pomades are mostly petroleum jelly, mineral oil or lanolin, often with beeswax for stiffness; water-based versions use polymers and hardening agents. Wax-type products stay pliable and hold hair in place without drying out like alcohol-heavy gels. The evidence base is mostly product descriptions and history, with no clinical studies.

paras: People work a small amount through towel-dried or dry hair with the hands or a comb and shape the style, choosing a heavier or lighter hold for the look they want. Oil-based products need repeated washes to remove; water-based ones rinse out more easily.

Wikipedia reports that some styling-product ingredients can strip oils or build up on hair, contributing to dryness, and that petroleum-based pomades can take several washes to remove; claims about follicle clogging or hair loss rest on non-clinical sources. A 2023 measurement study of Beijing hair salons found that styling products including clay, wax and gel release volatile organic compounds.

angle.text: Clay and pomade hold and texture hair so a style keeps its shape, giving a matte or slick finish visible immediately. They are styling aids for a neater, more put-together haircut through the day.

lead: Hair clay and pomade are styling products used to shape and hold hair. Pomade is a greasy, waxy or water-based product that gives a shiny, slick appearance, holds longer than most hair products and often takes repeated washes to remove [1]. Clay is a related category of styling product; general encyclopedic coverage of it is thin [2][3].

Traditional pomades were made from bear fat or lard in the 18th and 19th centuries, with petroleum jelly, beeswax and lard more common by the early 1900s [1]. Modern oil-based pomades typically contain lanolin, beeswax and petroleum jelly in heavy, medium or light holds, while water-based pomades use polymers and are easier to wash out [1]. The products are central to pompadour, quiff, ducktail and undercut styles [1].

No clinical studies of hair clay or pomade were found. The best available data concern emissions: a 2023 study sampled products in Beijing salons and measured their volatile organic compound output [4].
infobox: Oil-based pomade, water-based pomade, wax, clay, paste [1][3]
Petroleum jelly, mineral oil, lanolin, beeswax, polymers [1][3]

paras: Oil-based pomades contain ingredients such as lanolin, beeswax and petroleum jelly and come in heavy, medium and light holds; lighter versions, historically called brilliantine, are shinier and give a wet look [1]. Water-based gel pomades offer firm hold but are less malleable and often contain hardening agents, while some newer water-based pomades are designed to feel like oil-based ones but wash out easily [1].

Hair wax helps hold hair while staying pliable, and unlike gel, which mostly contains alcohol, is less likely to dry the hair out. It is sold under many names including pomade, putty, glue, whip, molding gum and styling paste, with texture and purpose varying by manufacturer [2]. Common waxes include beeswax, candelilla, carnauba, castor and japan wax, plus lanolin and ozokerite [2].

Wikipedia's article on styling products describes pomade as mostly petroleum jelly and mineral oil, often with wax, and notes that gel was popularised for spiky styles by punk culture in the 1980s [3]. Details of clay composition are not given in these general references.

Ancient Egyptians used a fat-based substance on hair, and the Gauls are said to have invented a waxy, soap-like styling agent [1][2]. Landmarks listed in Wikipedia's styling product article include Rowland's Macassar Oil in 1793, brilliantine in 1900 and Brylcreem in 1928 [3]. Morgan's Pomade was founded in the UK in 1873, and pomades were at their peak popularity from the 1920s to the 1950s, with brands including Murray's Superior Pomade (1925), Sweet Georgia Brown (1934) and Royal Crown (1936) [1].

The pompadour was associated with rock and roll in the mid-1950s and 1960s, worn by figures such as Elvis Presley, Chuck Berry and James Dean, and pomade returned in the 2010s alongside the undercut revival [1].

Wikipedia reports that most styling products do not damage hair when applied properly, but any styling product carries some risk of drying hair, and ingredients that strip natural oils or build up on hair may contribute to dryness or breakage [3]. Its pomade article says petroleum-based pomades can build up, clog follicles and possibly impede hair growth, but notes that these claims rely mainly on a hair-care retailer's blog rather than medical sources [1]. No clinical study of this was found.

A 2023 study measured volatile organic compound emissions from 88 hair products sampled across 139 Beijing salons and reported emission factors of about 78.9 g/kg for hair clay, 70.3 g/kg for hair wax and 156.4 g/kg for hair styling gel [4].
No studies found. Related work includes the 2023 salon emissions study of hair products, which is an environmental measurement rather than a clinical trial [4].
